title: RigorLLM: Resilient Guardrails for Large Language Models against Undesired Content
venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: The authors study harmful-content detection when an attacker tries to evade a guardrail. RigorLLM combines synthetic training-data generation, a defensive suffix and a fusion mechanism using nearest-neighbor classification and language models. Its evaluation includes ToxicChat and adversarially modified inputs, with comparisons against moderation services and other guardrails. The authors report stronger harmful-content detection and resilience within their experiments. These findings concern a multi-component defense, not a small standalone text classifier. For HMEG, the relevant idea is combining complementary evidence while evaluating robustness separately from ordinary classification. HMEG instead investigates detection-mechanism experts and confidence-based routing; it does not implement RigorLLM.
objective: Improve harmful-content detection and resilience to adversarial inputs.
methodology: Generate synthetic data using an energy-based model and Langevin dynamics; construct a defensive suffix with minimax optimization; fuse nearest-neighbor and language-model decisions.
datasets: Adversarial evaluation inputs described in the paper
results: The authors report stronger detection than evaluated baselines on their harmful-content and jailbreak settings. Consult the source tables for settings; these are not HMEG results.
opportunity: Test whether heterogeneous expert fusion improves HMEG robustness without the runtime cost of a multi-LLM guardrail.
findings: Data augmentation, defensive input transformation and prediction fusion are evaluated as complementary defenses.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
ensemble: Fusion of KNN and LLM predictions

title: DUALBREACH: Efficient Dual-Jailbreaking via Target-Driven Initialization and Multi-Target Optimization
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS 2026)
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: This paper examines whether a system remains safe when both its language model and its external guardrail are challenged together. The authors evaluate paired failures across protected model configurations and introduce EGUARD as a defensive response. EGUARD combines multiple guardrail outputs using XGBoost, so it is a learned fusion system rather than a new name for one classifier. The paper reports lower guardrail attack success with EGUARD than with Llama-Guard-3 in the evaluated settings. For HMEG, the useful connection is learned fusion and joint robustness testing. HMEG uses specialized detection-mechanism experts and hierarchical routing, which differs from ensembling existing guardrails.
objective: Evaluate joint vulnerabilities of LLMs and external guardrails, and investigate learned guardrail fusion.
methodology: Controlled robustness evaluation of protected LLM configurations; EGUARD learns an XGBoost ensemble over existing guardrail outputs.
results: Section I reports that EGUARD reduces guardrail attack success by up to 25% relative to Llama-Guard-3 in the studied settings. This is an attack-success comparison, not classifier accuracy.
opportunity: Evaluate the robustness of HMEG fusion against held-out attack mechanisms; distinguish this from a claim to reproduce EGUARD.
findings: Robustness of the LLM and its guardrail should be examined together; learned ensemble fusion is evaluated as a defense.
scopeNote: Attack-focused source: the diagram summarizes defensive evaluation only. EGUARD is a contribution within DUALBREACH, not a separate paper. HMEG currently evaluates English prompts only.
ensemble: EGUARD combines existing guardrails with XGBoost

title: Prompt Injection Detection and Mitigation via AI Multi-Agent NLP Frameworks
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: The authors investigate whether specialized language-model agents can detect and mitigate prompt injection during response generation. Their pipeline contains a generator, a guard or sanitizer, a policy enforcer and a metric evaluator. Agents exchange structured contextual information using the OVON messaging framework. The experiments use 500 synthetic injection prompts and Llama-family models, assessing injection success, policy outcomes and other custom indicators. The authors report improvements from the coordinated pipeline, while acknowledging limited human oversight and dependence on one model family. HMEG can draw evaluation ideas from this division of responsibilities, but its experts are supervised detectors rather than autonomous language-model agents.
objective: Detect and mitigate prompt injection using coordinated language-model agents.
methodology: A Llama 2 generator feeds Llama 3.1 guard/sanitizer and policy-enforcer agents; OVON JSON messages carry context and detection metadata; a separate evaluator measures outcomes.
datasets: 500 synthetic injection prompts generated with OpenAI o3-mini
results: The paper reports improvements in security and reliability using its custom multi-agent evaluation; no directly comparable HMEG accuracy is established.
limitations: The authors identify limited human oversight, limited agent diversity from the Llama family and simplified metadata exchange.
opportunity: Use complementary expert responsibilities while measuring whether extra stages justify their latency.
findings: Coordinated generation, sanitization and policy checking are evaluated as separate roles.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
ensemble: Coordinated multi-agent pipeline, not a classical classifier ensemble

title: GuardNet: Ensemble Strategies of Shallow Neural Networks for Robust Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Detection
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: GuardNet studies whether an ensemble of shallow neural classifiers can provide practical prompt-injection and jailbreak detection with modest inference cost. The model contains three independent bidirectional LSTM heads. The authors assess it on a blind JailbreakBench set and a small proprietary evaluation, while explicitly discussing partial information leakage and threshold calibration. They report a blind-test AUROC of 0.747 and a proprietary-set F1 of 0.92; these numbers come from different settings and should not be compared as equivalent evidence. For HMEG, the paper motivates flat ensemble baselines and careful calibration. HMEG investigates heterogeneous experts and selective deeper processing rather than a homogeneous recurrent ensemble.
objective: Investigate shallow neural ensembles for efficient prompt-injection and jailbreak detection.
methodology: Three shallow BiLSTM classifier heads form the GuardNet ensemble; evaluate calibration and robustness across blind and partially exposed evaluation settings.
datasets: Proprietary evaluation: 50 examples, with partial information leakage disclosed
results: Abstract: blind JBB AUROC 0.747; proprietary-set F1 0.92; CPU mean latency approximately 50 ms. The proprietary result includes partial information leakage and threshold calibration. Larger evaluated LLMs outperform GuardNet on blind F1/AUROC.
opportunity: Compare HMEG against flat fusion under a genuinely held-out protocol, and select thresholds only on validation data.
findings: The reported lightweight inference result comes with substantial differences between blind and partially exposed evaluation conditions.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.

title: SoK: Evaluating Jailbreak Guardrails for Large Language Models
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: This systematization organizes jailbreak guardrails and evaluates their security, efficiency and utility together. The authors classify defenses by intervention stage, technical approach, safety granularity, response behavior, applicability and explainability. They then examine how protection, computational cost and rejection of benign requests interact. Their analysis includes false-positive behavior on OR-Bench and shows that method labels alone do not establish a universal efficiency or safety ranking. Hardware-specific measurements and incomplete coverage of evolving attacks limit generalization. For HMEG, this motivates reporting latency, false positives and held-out attack performance alongside detection scores, instead of presenting one accuracy number as complete evidence of quality.
objective: Systematize guardrail mechanisms and evaluate their security-efficiency-utility trade-offs.
methodology: Six-dimensional taxonomy plus empirical assessment of guardrail security, latency/memory and benign-request utility.
datasets: Multiple jailbreak attack evaluations described in the source
results: The evaluation finds substantial variation in protection, resource costs and false positives across mechanisms. Figure 2 and the cross-attack analysis should be read with their specific settings; no universal ranking is inferred.
limitations: The authors note hardware-specific efficiency measurements on NVIDIA H800 GPUs and limits to exhaustive coverage of guardrail methods and evolving attacks.
opportunity: Measure HMEG false positives, routing cost and generalization within one controlled protocol.
findings: Guardrail comparisons require security, efficiency and benign-user utility to be assessed together.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.

title: LLM Jailbreak Detection for (Almost) Free!
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025, pp. 5777-5807
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: The authors investigate whether an aligned language model can help detect jailbreaks during its normal inference. Free Jailbreak Detection adds a short affirmative instruction and uses temperature-scaled first-token confidence as a detection signal. An extension learns a virtual instruction. Experiments cover Llama 2, Vicuna and Guanaco models, with AdvBench attacks and benign data from PureDove, Open-Platypus and SuperGLUE. The paper reports effective detection with little extra inference work, but also documents model sensitivity and detection-aware attacks. Its relevance to HMEG is the explicit study of confidence and computational overhead. HMEG uses classifier probabilities for routing and does not reproduce this internal-LLM method.
objective: Detect jailbreaks with minimal additional computation during LLM inference.
methodology: Prepend an affirmative instruction; temperature-scale output logits; use first-token confidence for detection. FJD-LI learns a virtual instruction.
results: The paper evaluates detection AUROC across models and attack types. The claimed small overhead applies to integration into the target LLM forward pass, not a standalone CPU classifier.
limitations: The authors report weaknesses against some non-readable prompts, detection-aware white-box attacks and model/version-dependent confidence behavior.
opportunity: Evaluate calibration and efficiency explicitly while keeping HMEG independent of target-LLM logits.
findings: First-token output confidence can supply an efficient detection signal under the studied settings.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
calibration: Temperature scaling; AUROC evaluates all thresholds

title: Comparative evaluation of machine learning methods for protecting LLMs from prompt injection attacks
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: The authors compare several ways to detect prompt injection: traditional classifiers using embeddings, independently fine-tuned transformers, existing specialized detectors and general language models. They select the jayavibhav/prompt-injection corpus, containing 327,400 queries, after reviewing four candidate datasets. Fine-tuned transformers provide strong balanced performance in this benchmark, while the traditional models differ considerably. For example, the reported LightGBM accuracy is 90.42% and random-forest accuracy is 83.07%. The authors warn that reliance on one balanced dataset limits real-world generalization. For HMEG, the paper supports using several standalone baselines and testing cross-source transfer. Its results are literature evidence, not measurements of HMEG.
objective: Compare four families of prompt-injection detectors under a shared benchmark.
methodology: Select a dataset with defined training and test partitions; compare embedding-based classifiers, fine-tuned transformers, specialized detectors and general LLMs.
datasets: jayavibhav/prompt-injection: 327,400 total queries, source-defined train/test partitions
results: Table 2: Naive Bayes accuracy 60.04%, LightGBM 90.42%, Random Forest 83.07%, MLP 96.80%, on the selected benchmark. These are published results and are not directly comparable with HMEG on a different dataset.
limitations: The authors identify single-dataset dependence, the difference between balanced benchmark and production prevalence, embedding-model variability, label coverage and lack of adaptive-attack evaluation.
opportunity: Compare HMEG against reproducible single-detector baselines and test source-held-out data rather than assuming benchmark transfer.
findings: Fine-tuned transformers perform strongly in the studied benchmark; classical and specialized detectors have different precision/recall trade-offs.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
steps: Evaluate accuracy, precision, recall and F1

title: WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, Datasets and Benchmarks Track
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: WildGuard addresses three related moderation tasks: identifying harmful user intent, judging harmful model responses and recognizing refusals. The authors construct WildGuardMix with 92,000 labeled examples and instruction-tune Mistral-7b-v0.3 for a unified output format. Evaluation covers WildGuardTest and multiple public safety benchmarks. The paper reports improvements across the three tasks, but notes that synthetic data, finite model coverage and differences in harm taxonomies can limit transfer. For HMEG, the useful lessons concern separating input risk from output harm, auditing synthetic-data coverage and measuring false refusals. HMEG remains an English input detector and does not implement WildGuard or its complete moderation workflow.
objective: Build an open moderation system covering prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness and refusal detection.
methodology: Construct a balanced multitask moderation dataset and instruction-tune Mistral-7b-v0.3 to produce three task-specific outputs.
features: User prompt and optional model response
datasets: WildGuardMix: 92K labeled examples across 13 risk categories
results: Table 3 reports WildGuard mean F1 86.1% for prompt harmfulness across five public benchmarks and 82.4% for response harmfulness across four public benchmarks. The tasks and datasets differ from HMEG evaluation.
limitations: The authors note heavy reliance on synthetic inputs, limited coverage of real user and model-response distributions, and differences between harm taxonomies.
opportunity: Keep HMEG jailbreak labels distinct from harmful-topic and refusal labels, and audit coverage of benign prompts.
findings: A unified safety model can address input harm, response harm and refusal detection, with task-specific evaluation.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.

title: SmoothLLM: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreaking Attacks
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: SmoothLLM explores a defense based on the sensitivity of adversarial prompts to small character changes. It creates perturbed copies of a prompt, queries the protected language model and aggregates the resulting safety judgments. The authors evaluate several jailbreak attack families on AdvBench and also examine normal instruction-following performance. Their experiments show robustness improvements in the studied conditions, with a trade-off: stronger perturbations can damage legitimate task performance. This motivates HMEG testing for unusual formatting while monitoring benign false positives. HMEG does not rewrite prompts or repeatedly query an LLM; its Format Expert classifies character-level evidence as one input to the guardrail.
objective: Mitigate jailbreaks through randomized prompt perturbation and aggregation.
methodology: Create multiple character-perturbed copies, query the target LLM and aggregate outputs according to safety judgments.
models: Protected LLMs including Llama 2 and Vicuna
results: The paper reports reduced attack success under the evaluated attacks. Figure 9 shows ordinary instruction-following degradation as perturbation strength increases; robustness should be read together with this utility trade-off.
limitations: The authors identify the trade-off between perturbation strength and nominal task performance, and note that safety judges can mislabel responses to heavily perturbed prompts.
opportunity: Measure HMEG robustness to character obfuscation without equating unusual formatting with malicious intent.
findings: Randomized transformations can improve resistance while also harming legitimate task utility.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
ensemble: Aggregate decisions from multiple perturbed prompt copies
steps: Select a compatible response or refusal

title: Detecting Language Model Attacks with Perplexity
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: The authors study machine-generated adversarial suffixes using GPT-2 perplexity and prompt length. They show why a simple perplexity cutoff can reject legitimate prompts, especially very short inputs with unusual token sequences. A LightGBM classifier combines length and perplexity, with its decision threshold selected on validation data using F2. In the reported test, the classifier detects many generated suffix attacks but misses all 23 human-crafted jailbreak examples. This is evidence for a specialized structural signal, not a universal jailbreak detector. For HMEG, it motivates combining the Pattern Expert with semantic and instruction experts and explicitly testing short benign prompts.
objective: Detect machine-generated adversarial suffix prompts while reducing false positives from perplexity-only rules.
methodology: Compute GPT-2 perplexity and sequence length; train LightGBM; tune the threshold on a separate validation set for F2; evaluate a held-out test set.
datasets: Regular prompt datasets described in the source
results: Table 1: 355 detected machine-generated attacks, 4 missed, and 23/23 human-crafted examples missed. Table 2: overall test F2 94.2%; F2 99.1% when human-crafted examples are excluded. These results cannot support a general jailbreak-detection claim.
limitations: The authors note incomplete coverage of real interactions, dependence on one attack-generation setup and exclusive use of GPT-2 for perplexity. The method does not detect the studied human-crafted jailbreaks.
opportunity: Combine structural evidence with other HMEG experts and audit short-prompt false positives separately.
findings: Prompt length helps distinguish some short benign high-perplexity inputs from adversarial suffixes; structural signals alone miss human-crafted attacks.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.

title: Benchmarking and Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2025)
abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
summary: BIPIA studies attacks hidden in external material that an LLM application reads while completing a legitimate task. The benchmark covers five application scenarios and 250 attacker goals, and the authors evaluate 25 language models. They identify confusion between data and instructions as a central weakness. Their defenses encourage boundary awareness and explicitly remind the model not to follow instructions embedded in untrusted content, with approaches for both black-box and white-box settings. The paper reports vulnerability across evaluated models and improvements from the defenses. For HMEG, this motivates source-aware instruction-manipulation tests; it does not establish that classifying isolated prompts provides complete application-level protection.
objective: Benchmark indirect prompt injection and investigate defenses that distinguish external content from legitimate instructions.
methodology: Build BIPIA application scenarios; evaluate protected tasks under injected external content; test boundary-awareness and explicit-reminder defenses.
models: 25 evaluated LLMs, including GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4
datasets: BIPIA: five application scenarios and 250 attacker goals
results: The paper reports varying susceptibility across the 25 evaluated LLMs and reduced attack success with boundary-awareness and explicit-reminder defenses. This is application-level indirect-injection evaluation, not binary prompt accuracy.
opportunity: Evaluate HMEG instruction-manipulation signals with explicit trusted/untrusted context and report the limits of isolated-prompt classification.
findings: Separating informational context from actionable instructions is central to indirect-injection defense.
scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
steps: Legitimate task and untrusted external content
Explicit instruction to ignore embedded commands
Measure injection success and task utility
